I'll write about something that has been occupying my thoughts lately: the quiet revolution happening in how we understand attention, memory, and the architecture of human experience in an age of digital abundance.

---

## The Architecture of Attention in an Age of Abundance

There is a peculiar phenomenon that occurs when you stand at the edge of the ocean at night, particularly if you have traveled far from the light pollution of cities. The darkness becomes almost tactile, a presence rather than an absence, and the sound of waves establishes a rhythm that seems to predate consciousness itself. In these moments, something shifts in the quality of one's attention. The mind, accustomed to the fractured, staccato demands of contemporary life, gradually unclenches. Thoughts begin to move differently—slower, perhaps, but also more deeply, as if descending through layers of water rather than skimming across surfaces.

I begin with this image because I believe it represents something we are in danger of losing, not through any dramatic catastrophe but through the slow accumulation of small choices, the gradual normalization of a particular way of being that we have not adequately examined. We are living through a transformation in the fundamental conditions of human attention, and we have barely begun to understand what this means.

Consider the history of attention as a concept. For most of human history, attention was not something one managed; it was simply something one possessed, like breath or heartbeat. The farmer watching for signs of rain, the hunter tracking prey through broken undergrowth, the mother listening for her infant's cry in the night—these forms of attention were embedded in immediate contexts, responsive to real and pressing demands. The attention was *called forth* by the world, drawn out by necessity and danger and care.

The problems of attention in earlier eras were problems of scarcity. The medieval monk struggling to maintain focus during prayer, the scholar in a library with limited texts, the apprentice learning to watch a master at work—these individuals faced the challenge of sustaining attention when the world offered little stimulation, when the mind wandered not toward distraction but toward emptiness. The solutions developed over centuries—the liturgical hour, the scholarly method, the craft tradition—were technologies for *generating* and *holding* attention in conditions of relative poverty.

What we face now is historically unprecedented: a problem of attentional abundance. The contemporary environment does not ask us to generate attention; it demands that we *defend* it, constantly, against an overwhelming tide of stimuli designed by some of the most sophisticated psychological and technological systems ever developed to capture and hold our gaze. The notification, the infinite scroll, the autoplay video, the recommended next article—these are not neutral tools but engineered environments that exploit known vulnerabilities in human cognitive architecture.

The psychologist Daniel Kahneman's distinction between fast and slow thinking has become widely known, but I think we need a more nuanced vocabulary for what is happening to attention. It is not merely that we are thinking fast rather than slow. It is that the *texture* of consciousness itself is changing, the way that time is experienced internally, the relationship between present experience and memory, the very sense of what it means to be a continuous self moving through a continuous world.

I have been conducting an informal experiment for several years now, one that I never designed formally but that emerged from a personal crisis of attention. I began to notice that my reading had changed—not just the amount, but the *quality*. I would sit with a book and find myself reaching for my phone after a few pages, not because I was bored with the book but because some part of my mind had become accustomed to interruption, had begun to *expect* it, to feel anxious in its absence. The sustained, linear engagement that serious reading requires had become uncomfortable, like a muscle that has atrophied and now protests when called upon.

So I began to make small resistances. I started reading physical books again, deliberately, in dedicated spaces without devices. I took up handwriting in a journal, forcing my thoughts to move at the speed of pen across paper rather than the speed of typing. I began taking long walks without headphones, without podcasts or music, simply attending to the environment through which I moved. These were not ascetic practices chosen for moral superiority; they were desperate attempts to recover something I felt I was losing, something I could not quite name.

What I have slowly come to understand is that I was trying to recover a particular temporal rhythm, a way of being in time that allows for what I want to call *depth*. The philosopher Byung-Chul Han has written about what he calls "contemplative time," contrasting it with the "narrative time" of digital media. In narrative time, each moment exists primarily as a transition to the next, a link in a chain that is always pulling forward. The tweet leads to the thread, the thread to the article, the article to the next article, in an endless succession that never quite arrives anywhere. Contemplative time, by contrast, allows moments to *expand*, to become thick with meaning and connection, to resonate with what came before and what might come after in ways that are not merely sequential but associative, emotional, even spiritual.

This distinction helps me understand what I experienced in those early days of deliberate attentional practice. When I first sat with a book and forced myself to remain with it, to resist the urge to check, to refresh, to move on, the experience was genuinely uncomfortable. There was a kind of anxiety, a restless energy that sought outlet. But if I persisted, something would eventually shift. The reading would become *absorptive* rather than *extractive*—I was no longer mining the text for information, for something I could use or share, but entering into a relationship with it, allowing it to work upon me slowly, cumulatively, in ways that might not become apparent for days or weeks.

The French philosopher Simone Weil wrote that "attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity." This is a radical claim in our context, where attention is so often understood as a resource to be allocated, a commodity to be traded, a currency in the attention economy. Weil suggests something different: that attention is a gift we give to reality, an opening of the self to what is other than the self. In genuine attention, there is a kind of surrender, a willingness to be affected, to be changed, to be surprised. This is precisely what the engineered environments of digital media are designed to prevent. The algorithm knows what you have liked before and offers more of the same. The surprise is carefully controlled, the affect carefully managed. There is no genuine otherness, only the simulation of otherness that leads back to the same.

I want to be careful here not to romanticize a pre-digital past or to suggest that all technology is harmful. The printing press was once revolutionary, and it transformed attention in its own ways. The novel, as a form, created new possibilities for sustained imaginative engagement that did not exist before. Radio, cinema, television—each introduced new temporal rhythms, new forms of attention and distraction. What seems different about the current transformation is the *pervasiveness* and *personalization* of the attentional environment. It is not that we occasionally visit a distracting medium; it is that we carry the medium with us, that it has become the environment in which most of our waking life occurs.

The implications for memory are profound and, I think, underexplored. We know from cognitive science that memory is not a simple recording but a constructive process, deeply dependent on attention. The moments we attend to are the moments that become available for later recollection. The quality of our attention determines the quality of our memory. What, then, does it mean to live in a state of continuous partial attention, of perpetual distraction? It means, I believe, that our memories themselves become thinner, more fragmented, less woven into a coherent narrative of a life.

I have noticed this in my own experience. The years when I was most immersed in digital media, most constantly connected, are years I struggle to remember with any specificity. They blur together, a continuous present of similar stimuli producing similar responses. The years when I have been more deliberate about attention—when I have traveled, when I have maintained practices of reading and writing and walking—are years that feel *denser* in memory, more eventful not because more happened but because more was *noticed*, more was *registered*, more was *integrated* into the ongoing story of a self.

The philosopher Alasdair MacIntyre has argued that human beings are essentially storytelling animals, that we understand our lives and ourselves through narrative. If this is true, then the attentional crisis is also a crisis of selfhood, of identity, of meaning. The self that cannot attend cannot narrate; the self that cannot narrate cannot, in a full sense, *be*. This may sound overly dramatic, but I think the phenomenology supports it. There is a kind of hollowing out that occurs in lives of perpetual distraction, a sense of watching oneself live rather than actually living, of being always at one remove from one's own experience.

What, then, is to be done? I do not think the answer is simple renunciation, a return to some imagined pre-technological innocence. The digital world is not going away, and it offers genuine goods—connection across distance, access to information, tools for creativity and collaboration. The question is not whether to engage with it but *how*, on what terms, with what awareness of its costs and benefits.

I have come to think of attention as a kind of ecological resource, like clean water or fertile soil. It can be depleted through overuse, polluted through exposure to toxins, restored through careful stewardship. This means thinking not just about individual practices but about collective ones, about the environments we create and inhabit together. It means asking questions about design, about regulation, about the social norms that shape what is acceptable and expected.

At the individual level, I have found value in what I think of as *attentional rituals*—practices that mark transitions between different modes of engagement, that create boundaries and containers for different kinds of attention. The morning without screens, the dedicated reading time, the walk without headphones, the evening conversation without phones on the table—these are small acts of environmental design, attempts to create spaces where a different kind of attention can flourish.

I have also found value in what I want to call *attentional slowness*, a deliberate resistance to the acceleration that characterizes so much contemporary experience. This is not mere nostalgia for a slower past; it is a recognition that some things require time to unfold, that understanding is often gradual and cumulative, that the demand for immediate comprehension is often a demand for superficiality. The slow reading of a difficult text, the slow observation of a natural phenomenon, the slow development of a relationship or a skill—these are forms of resistance to the temporal regime of the attention economy.

There is something here, too, about the body and its role in attention. The digital attentional environment is peculiarly disembodied, a realm of eyes and fingers, of scrolling and clicking, of a body held in more or less fixed position while the mind is supposedly transported elsewhere. The forms of attention I have been trying to recover are more fully embodied—walking, writing by hand, attending to breath and posture in meditation or prayer. The body, with its own temporal rhythms, its own slownesses and limitations, becomes a resource for attentional resistance, a way of grounding consciousness in something other than the digital flow.

I want to conclude by returning to the ocean at night with which I began, because I think it represents something important about what attention can be and what we risk losing. The ocean does not demand attention in the way a notification does. It does not exploit psychological vulnerabilities or offer variable rewards. It simply *is*, in its vastness and indifference, and in that is-ness it offers something that no designed environment can provide: genuine otherness, the encounter with something that does not care about us, that was not made for us, that exceeds our comprehension and our use.

This is, I think, what Weil meant by attention as generosity. To attend to the ocean, to the difficult book, to the friend in conversation, to the work of art or the natural world, is to acknowledge that these things have reality independent of our desires, that they make claims upon us that we can choose to honor or ignore. The attention economy teaches us to see everything as resource, as potential content, as material for our own self-construction and self-promotion. Genuine attention teaches something different: that the world is not merely raw material for our projects, but a presence that can address us, challenge us, change us, if we allow it to do so.

The question of our time, I believe, is whether we can develop forms of life that sustain this kind of attention, that protect it against the powerful forces arrayed against it, that make it available not just as individual privilege but as common good. This is not a matter of personal virtue alone, though personal practices matter. It is a matter of collective choice, of the institutions and environments we build together, of the kind of civilization we want to become.

We are, perhaps, at a turning point. The early enthusiasm for digital technology, the utopian promises of connection and democratization, have given way to a more sober reckoning with costs and consequences. The conversation is changing, and with it the possibility of different choices. What we need now is not rejection but discernment, not denial but wisdom—the wisdom to know what serves genuine human flourishing and what undermines it, the courage to build lives and societies that reflect this knowledge.

The ocean waits, indifferent to our choices. But we do not wait for ourselves. The attention we give or withhold, the presence we offer or refuse, the depth we cultivate or abandon—these are the materials from which our lives are made, the legacy we leave to those who come after. In the end, there is nothing more urgent, and nothing more worthy of our attention, than the question of attention itself.
